caption:
Most people are living
inside a story
where they gave more
than they received.

Where they were less seen
than they deserved.

Where the people around them
failed to meet their needs.

Some of that is true.

All of it is incomplete.

Japanese psychologists
developed a method
in the 1940s
that produced complete remission
of depression in patients
who had not responded
to any other treatment.

It is called Naikan.

And it works
by asking three questions
about every significant relationship
in your life.

What did this person do for me.
What did I do for them.
What trouble did I cause them.

The third question
is where most people go silent.

Because the honest answer
is almost always
more than they expected.

And the second question
is where most people discover
their giving
was smaller than their memory
made it.

The victim narrative
requires enormous energy
to maintain.

Every day
you must remember the evidence.
Rehearse the justifications.
Protect the story
from anything
that contradicts it.

Naikan dissolves the narrative
not by denying the harm
but by restoring the context
the pain removed.

When you see clearly
that you were also loved.
That you also caused harm.
That you were also given to.

The story of being
only wronged
becomes impossible to sustain.

And the energy spent maintaining it
comes flooding back.

Clinical research
at Kyushu University found
that patients who completed Naikan
showed significant reduction
in depression
and measurably improved
relationship quality.

Not because their relationships changed.

Because they did.
